contexts.name: Orders
contexts.responsibility: Owns an order from draft through fulfilment; nothing else may write order state

contexts.name: Billing
contexts.responsibility: Owns invoices, payments and dunning; the only context allowed to talk to the payment provider

contexts.name: Catalog
contexts.responsibility: Owns products, prices and availability as published to buyers

contexts.name: Identity
contexts.responsibility: Owns accounts, org membership and permissions; issues the tokens every other context verifies

contexts.name: Notifications
contexts.responsibility: Owns delivery of email and webhooks, including retry and suppression; holds no business state

integrations.failureBehaviour: Serve the last-known price from a 60s cache and mark the quote provisional; refuse to place an order priced from stale data older than 15 minutes
Reject with 401 rather than assuming a permission; cached JWKS lets verification survive a short outage

integrations.contract: order.placed v1 (outbox → broker), consumer-driven contract test
Nightly price snapshot for revenue reporting

patterns.name: Transactional outbox
patterns.problem: An order must never be committed without its event; writing to the database and the broker separately loses one of them whenever the process dies in between
patterns.cost: A relay process to operate, an outbox table that grows and needs pruning, and at-least-once delivery that forces idempotent consumers

patterns.name: Anti-corruption layer
patterns.problem: The payment provider's model leaks refunds, disputes and partial captures into our domain, and their vocabulary would spread through the codebase within a quarter
patterns.cost: A translation layer to maintain and a second model to keep in sync when the provider changes

patterns.name: Read replica for reporting
patterns.problem: Analytical queries over invoices were competing with payment writes and causing lock contention during month-end
patterns.cost: Replication lag makes reports eventually consistent, which the finance team must be told about explicitly

adrs.title: Split billing from orders
adrs.context: One deploy pipeline blocked both teams, and a billing migration once stopped order intake for 40 minutes despite orders being healthy
adrs.decision: Separate bounded contexts with their own datastores, integrated asynchronously
adrs.consequences: Order state and invoice state are eventually consistent; support needs a joined read model, and month-end reconciliation becomes an explicit job rather than a join

adrs.title: Orders → billing is asynchronous
adrs.context: Synchronous billing calls made order placement fail whenever the payment provider was slow, so a provider incident became an outage for the whole funnel
adrs.decision: Orders publish order.placed via the outbox; billing consumes it
adrs.consequences: Invoices appear seconds after the order; billing must be idempotent on event id, and the customer sees 'invoice pending' in the UI for that window

adrs.title: Catalog reads stay synchronous
adrs.context: Prices must be current at quote time and staleness is directly visible to buyers, so an eventually consistent copy would be wrong in the one moment that matters
adrs.decision: Synchronous read with a short cache and an explicit degraded mode
adrs.consequences: Orders degrade to provisional quotes when catalog is down rather than failing outright, and we accept a hard dependency on catalog availability during quoting

adrs.title: Shared 'platform' database
adrs.context: The original monolith kept every table in one schema, which made cross-domain joins trivial and ownership impossible
adrs.decision: Keep one database for all services
adrs.consequences: Any team could migrate any table, so nobody owned the schema; two incidents were traced to a migration run by a team that did not know who else read the table
